story_text.value:
Hi all! I made a 311 byte Klotski solver in C++

So back when I first got to use a mobile phone in 2012 I used to play a lot of puzzle games. These were notoriously hard to solve (on high levels), and I always wondered how are these created, how do they find the minimum moves, how do they know its even minimal.

Now after being in a CS major for over 3 years, I finally understand these systems fairly. So I decided to make a klotski solver.

I wanted to make it fun so I stored the whole game board in an integer (uint64_t), as I like integers more than vectors. And then I got the urge to minify the engine to the max extent I could, so shrunk it down to 311 bytes from ~3.5 KB. The engine is only the searching part though.

The solver is a BFS that explores every reachable position. For the classic start it finds the best solution in 116 moves, after exploring all 25,955 reachable states in about 2-4 ms.

Here's the repo; any feedback is welcomed : ) https://github.com/Dream-World-Coder/depuzzled

title.value: Show HN: A 311 byte Klotski solver in C++

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Demetrius.

When OpenAI launched Dots (always-on agents in ChatGPT that run in the background, connect to your apps, and ask before risky actions), I wanted to set one up and went looking for examples of what other people were telling theirs. I couldn't find any.

Each Dot comes down to three things: its instructions, the apps it can reach, and Custom Rules (Allow / Require approval / Block). The rules matter most, because they decide what the agent does without asking you. They're also the part nobody was sharing.

So I built DotBotDirectory.

Each entry has the Dot's job, its instructions, its connected apps, and its three rule lists. One click copies the instructions and rules together so you can paste them into your own Dot.

Where it stands:

- 26 starter entries, written by me from ideas people published in early Dot write-ups. Each one credits its source.

- None of them have been tested on a real Dot yet, and they're labelled "Starter - untested". I'll mark entries as tested once someone confirms one works.

- Copy counts start at zero, so nothing looks more popular than it is.

- Free, and not affiliated with OpenAI.

Two questions for anyone who has run a Dot:

1. What did you put in Require approval vs Block? That's where I think most of the value is.

2. Did your Dot ever do something you didn't expect? I'd like to turn those cases into rules other people can copy.

Happy to answer anything.

title.value: Show HN: I built a directory to set up ChatGPT's always-on agents in one paste

story_text.value:
I built Smartly because I kept knowing what I wanted to do in the terminal—but forgetting the exact syntax and flags.

Smartly turns plain English into shell commands, using your OS, current directory, and Git context to help produce something relevant to where you’re working. It saves the back-and-forth of copying commands from an LLM into your terminal. It also supports Claude Code and Codex CLI if you already use those with a subscription.

There’s also a --learn mode for when you want to understand the command, not just get it done.

I’d love feedback. Thanks!

story_text.value:
https://chat.hesamian.com

https://github.com/amir734jj/symmetric-crypto-chat-room

I started working on this many years ago and incrementally improved this over-time. The idea is if two people choose a (channel + encryption key) then they should be able to communicate with each other (text, file, audio, video) fully encrypted all in your browser. The "server" just relays the data. It doesn't know what is being send/received.

If you join the channel with wrong encryption key, you will just receive garbage data.

title.value: Show HN: Symmetric encrypted chat (text, file, audio, video) in browser

story_text.value:
Hi HN! I've made it possible for you to make product roadmaps like you'd make an RPG skill tree, or a tech tree in a video game.

Ever since seeing WoW talent trees* in high school i've been obsessed with RPG skill trees as a way to represent information as I've thought they convey 1) Ordering, 2) Progression and 3) Contingent Requirements really well. Not only do they help give better visual structure of whats happening and what will happen - they also give people a feeling of movement, progression and hope (whereas kanban boards and issue trackers give people the feeling of dread).

This isn't surprising as video games were really designed to make people excited to play on and reach the next milestone.

Turns out this format is really fun for people and agents to think about their products! As an experiment I also hooked up an MCP to one of my product roadmaps and it was able to map out my current codebase to a kanmap, and then suggest realistic next ideas to make. I've even got an agent now working on the next node of a kanmap.

* Kanmaps was inspired not just by WOW talent trees, but also by the Age of Empires Tech Trees, and FFX ability spheres setup. Also huge shoutout to a bank in Australia called Up who did something called the Tree of Up as a product roadmap like a video game for their banking product - their work definitely inspired things in Kanmaps too.

title.value: Show HN: Kanmaps – Product roadmaps like videogame skill trees

kitdecoder.com runs entirely in the browser. I kept adding tools, around 28 now.

story_text.value:
Almost a year has passed since Desbordante’s last release, and now we’re rolling out a new one — 2.5.0.

Desbordante is an open-source, high-performance data profiler that finds and validates complex patterns in data using a bunch of advanced algorithms.

Unlike the black-box ML approaches that dominate today, Desbordante takes a symbolic, explainable approach to data analysis, producing explicit rules or rule-shaped artifacts that are verifiable, such as data dependencies, association rules, or other patterns. It’s a different way to analyze data, and it works well alongside black-box models. Unlike free-form model output, these patterns have precise semantics and can be validated algorithmically against the data. And, importantly, no hallucinations or misclassification.

This release adds 9 new patterns, including support for another dataset type: sequences in data. That brings the total to 4. We also picked up Python 3.15, which just came out. On top of the new patterns, there was a lot of infrastructure work too — mostly invisible to users, but important.

Full changelog: https://github.com/Desbordante/desbordante-core/releases/tag...

title.value: Show HN: Desbordante 2.5.0 Released
